reconcile.connective: Harmonizers separate 'lying wonders' tied to false doctrine from 'true miracles': a wonder credentials divine mission only when it seals truth already revealed.

discrepancy.connective: Baruch Spinoza cites Deuteronomy 13 to argue miracles prove nothing: since false prophets can also work signs, wonders cannot certify true divine mission.

skeptic.name: Baruch Spinoza
skeptic.work: Tractatus Theologico-Politicus (A Theologico-Political Treatise), ch. 6, "Of Miracles"
skeptic.attribution: Baruch Spinoza (1632-1677), Tractatus Theologico-Politicus, ch. 6, "Of Miracles" (1670)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Miracles are therefore the broad seal of heaven, and the doctrine they are affixed to must be of God, for his power will never contradict his truth; nor can it be imagined that he should set his seal to a lie; however lying wonders may be vouched for in proof of false doctrines, true miracles evince a divine commission; such Christ's were, and they leave no room to doubt that he was sent of God, and that his doctrine was his that sent him.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry's distinction between 'lying wonders' (which prop up false doctrine, as with Pharaoh's magicians or a Deut 13 false prophet) and 'true miracles' (which evince divine commission, as with Christ's) is the harmonizing move that directly answers the tension between the two verse-sets.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714), on Matthew 11:1-6
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly, distinguishing 'lying wonders' vouched for false doctrine from 'true miracles' that evince a divine commission -- the harmonizing principle answering the Exodus/Deuteronomy texts.
